title: The Microscope That Made Curiosity Independent

scenes.text: The first thing I remember about my microscope is not a spectacular discovery. It is how much I wanted an instrument that belonged to my own questions.
In Cairo, near Qasr El Einy, I found one. It was a simple decision to make, and a much less simple object to bring back with me.
Getting it to Qatar was a hassle. But the point was never to collect equipment. I wanted the freedom to look at something the moment curiosity appeared.
On the first of July, twenty seventeen, I posted a photograph. There it was on my desk in Qatar, surrounded by books, notes, and an American Chemical Society mug.
In a university laboratory, the schedule matters. You book an instrument, follow a method, respect the shared space. At home, I could return to a question without asking for an appointment.
A vacation morning could become an hour at the microscope. I could leave a slide on the stage, come back later, and look again. No deadline made the observation worthwhile.
Sometimes the most useful part was not what appeared in the eyepiece, but the act of looking twice: changing the focus, noticing what I missed, admitting I did not yet understand.
A microscope makes a small thing visible. It does not explain it. That takes comparisons, controls, patience, and other people who are willing to question what you think you saw.
I would not claim that this little microscope produced my later research results. Those belonged to teams and proper laboratories. What it gave me was different: a habit of paying attention.
I brought a microscope out of Cairo. What I really brought home was time: time to wonder, time to be wrong, and the freedom to look again.
